prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The five views show a furnished living room, with nearby furniture and people appearing bright in the lower foreground and the far wall, windows, television, and cabinets darker behind them. Across the strip, people are roughly 0.5–2 m from the camera wearer, foreground table or chair edges are within about 0.3–1 m, and the television and far wall are approximately 2–4 m away; the camera turns right, so previously central people and objects move left or leave view while two seated people and one standing person enter on the right. The map makes foreground occlusions clearer than RGB, including people and furniture blocking parts of the room, but it does not reliably separate adjacent people from nearby chairs or tables and gives poor depth around silhouettes, windows, and dark regions. Metric distances remain approximate because this is relative monocular depth, and the map alone does not reliably show gaze direction or whether someone faces the camera wearer.
descriptions.segmentation: The masks identify several people, televisions, chairs, a bowl, and—unreliably—a large central region labelled train or bus, while also showing which instances overlap or are partly outside the frame. Early frames place two overlapping people about 0.5–1.5 m ahead near the centre-right, with a television roughly 2–4 m away on the left; later frames place a seated person and chair about 1–2 m ahead-right and a standing person partly cut off at the far right, with people mutually separated by roughly 0.3–1 m. As the camera pans right, the early people move out to the left, the television reappears at different horizontal positions, and the right-side group becomes prominent; mask overlap shows that nearer bodies and chairs occlude one another. The map clarifies object identities and boundaries that are blurred in RGB, but the bus/train labels are clear misclassifications, several masks merge people with furniture, many room surfaces are omitted, and it provides no dependable facing, gaze, or precise metric depth.
descriptions.pose: The pose strip is entirely black, so it supplies no detected body or hand skeletons in any of the five frames and cannot establish limb positions, facing direction, gaze, reach, or person-to-person geometry. The RGB and other maps contain people at roughly 0.5–2 m and nearby furniture within possible arm-scale distance, but none of those spatial relations is encoded or independently supported by this pose map. It also shows no temporal change such as approach, retreat, or turning, despite the camera’s rightward viewpoint change visible elsewhere. The absence of detections is unreliable evidence rather than evidence that no people or hands are present, likely reflecting missed, occluded, blurred, or partly out-of-frame bodies.
